source_text: Nobis igitur in praesenti convincenda primo est sensus vestri hebetudo; tum ostendendum quod saepe iam fecimus, ne uno quidem pede a Manichaeorum vos gurgustiis meritoriisque discedere. Initio igitur, amentissimum est arbitrii negotium seminibus immixtum putare, et officia voluntatum inolevisse conceptibus; ut ea, quae est clarissima atque vastissima, naturarum et studiorum distinctione sublata, voluntas primorum posteris se ingenuisse dicatur. Cui errori obluctatur quidquid in rebus est. Numquam siquidem filii disertorum venustatem artis paternae in vagitibus attulerunt, aut soboles histrionum doctis motibus ad verba manus tetendit; nec bellatorum filii tubam populo poposcerunt. Licet hac forma, exempla omnium persequi clariora tonitribus concinentia. Respondebit universitas alios esse naturae limites, alios voluntatis; conditionesque seminum studiorum appetitibus pervias esse non posse. Bardissimum itaque et depositae stoliditatis apparuit credere conversum in naturam, quod voluntarium fuisse fateare. Ceterum illud aliud longe longeque deformius, quod possibilitatem operandi initio ais operationis assumptam, id est, ut liberum arbitrium (quod non est aliud quam possibilitas peccandi et non peccandi, nulli partis alterutrae subdita violentiae, sed quae habeat facultatem in quod voluerit latus suopte insistendi arbitratu), postquam coepit alterum velle, utrumque posse perdiderit.
pass_a_gloss: For us therefore in the present first the dullness of your sense must be convicted; then it must be shown what we have often already done, that you do not recede even by one foot from the huts and lodgings of the Manichaeans. In the beginning therefore it is most mad to think the business of decision mixed into seeds, and the offices of wills to have grown into conceptions; so that that distinction of natures and of studies, which is most clear and most vast, having been taken away, the will of the first is said to have generated itself into posterity. Whatever is in things struggles against this error. For never have the sons of the eloquent brought the charm of paternal art in wailings, or has the offspring of actors stretched hands to words with learned motions; nor have the sons of warriors demanded a trumpet from the people. It is allowed by this form to pursue examples of all, clearer than thunders, agreeing. The universe will reply that there are other limits of nature, others of will; and that the conditions of seeds cannot be passable to the appetites of studies. It has therefore appeared most dull and of a laid-down stolidity to believe converted into nature what you confess was voluntary. For the rest that other thing far far more deformed, that you say a possibility of working was taken up at the beginning of the operation, that is, that free decision (which is nothing other than a possibility of sinning and of not sinning, subjected to the violence of neither part, but which has a faculty of insisting by its own judgment toward which side it has willed), after it began to will one, lost being able both.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS meritum; Blaise; glossary: desert not treasury-of-merit

pass_b_english: For the present, then, we must first expose the dullness of your thinking, and then show—as we have often done already—that you never step even one foot away from the Manichaeans’ hovels and brothels. To begin with, it is utterly mad to think an act of choice was mixed into reproductive seed and the operations of wills took root in conceptions. You abolish the clearest and widest distinction between natures and pursuits, and then say the first humans’ will reproduced itself in their descendants. Everything in existence struggles against this error.

Orators’ sons never brought the elegance of their fathers’ art into their infant cries; actors’ offspring did not stretch their hands in trained gestures to accompany words; warriors’ sons did not demand a trumpet from the crowd. We may pursue examples of every kind on this pattern, all sounding together more clearly than thunder. The whole of things answers that nature has one set of boundaries, will another, and the conditions of reproductive seed cannot be penetrated by the desires of chosen pursuits. It has therefore proved a belief of the dullest, most abject stupidity to think that something admittedly voluntary was transformed into nature.

But your other claim is far, far more disgraceful: you say the capacity to act was consumed when action began. Free will is simply the capacity to sin and not to sin, subject to no compulsion on either side, but able by its own choice to stand on whichever side it wants. Yet you say that once it began to will one side, it lost the ability to choose either.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
